column1: sam-domain|E|E4|ad|Why is a workstation's local SAM not a complete domain credential database?|Local and domain account authorities are separate|Every domain password is stored only in DNS|The SAM stores only network packet captures|The workstation has no local account identifiers|Domain directory data belongs to AD; local accounts belong to the machine authority. Cached domain logon material is yet another artifact.|Distinguish local accounts, directory accounts, and cached credentials.

sid-authority|E|E2|ad|Two accounts end in RID 1001 but have different SID authority prefixes. What follows?|They are different security principals|They must be the same account with two names|Both must be domain administrators|Both necessarily share a password hash|A RID is relative to its issuing authority. Comparing only the final component loses identity information.|A relative identifier needs its authority context.

guest-rid|E|E2|ad|Which conventional RID identifies the built-in Guest account?|501|500|512|1000|501 identifies Guest within the relevant authority. 500 identifies the built-in Administrator; a group RID has a different role.|Account and group identifiers are not interchangeable.

admin-member|E|E5|ad|A user belongs to Administrators but a process has a restricted token. What must be assessed?|The process's effective token and elevation state|Only the account's display name|Only the host's registered DNS suffix|Only whether a desktop shortcut exists|Group membership does not fully describe the running token. UAC and process context can affect effective authority.|Account membership and process privilege differ.

group-recursion|E|E2|ad|Why inspect nested group membership when assessing domain privileges?|Indirect memberships may grant effective rights|Every nested group disables all inherited access|Groups can contain only local users|A group name uniquely identifies its SID worldwide|Effective rights can arise through nesting. Group scope, membership, and token construction influence applicability.|A direct-members-only listing may miss authority.

ldap-base|E|E2|ldap|An LDAP search uses a base under one OU. Why might it miss users in another OU?|The search scope does not include that subtree|LDAP returns every directory entry regardless of base|The other OU necessarily has no users|All user accounts must reside in the queried OU|Search base and scope define the candidate region. An empty result is not a domain-wide absence claim.|Enumeration has a search boundary.

gc-purpose|E|E3|ad|What is the Active Directory Global Catalog intended to support?|Forest-wide discovery using a partial attribute view|Replacement of all domain-controller authentication|A public list of every password hash|Storage of only the host's local SAM|The GC provides searchable forest information with selected attributes. It does not expose every directory value or replace all DC functions.|Wide object coverage need not mean full attribute coverage.

rid-master|E|E3|ad|Which FSMO role allocates RID pools to domain controllers?|RID Master|PDC Emulator|Schema Master|Domain Naming Master|RID allocation helps DCs create unique security identifiers within a domain. Other roles manage different directory operations.|Know which single-master responsibility matches the operation.

schema-master|E|E3|ad|Which FSMO role controls schema changes?|Schema Master|Infrastructure Master|RID Master|PDC Emulator|Schema changes modify definitions used by directory objects. This is a forest-wide role, distinct from RID allocation.|Forest-wide and domain-wide responsibilities differ.

pdc-role|E|E3|ad|Why is the PDC Emulator relevant to password and time-related assessment?|It has special domain roles in password updates and time hierarchy|It is every workstation's only DNS resolver|It exposes all group-policy files anonymously|It replaces every Kerberos service ticket|The role is relevant to domain operations, but the exact authentication path and policy still need verification.|A special role does not make every request pass through one server.

sysvol-write|E|E3|ad|A low-privilege account can modify a script in SYSVOL that runs for administrators. Which trust boundary is threatened?|Low-privilege write into higher-privilege execution|Browser rendering into DNS delegation|SMTP relay into TLS certificate validation|Anonymous FTP into wireless authentication|The script's consumers and execution context matter. An expected read share can become dangerous with unauthorized write access.|Assess who can write and who later executes.

policy-link|E|E3|ad|A GPO exists but is not linked to an affected OU. Why does its presence not prove enforcement?|Existence and application scope are different|Every GPO applies to every domain object|Only the file's name determines its scope|A GPO link always overrides all filtering|Linking, inheritance, filtering, and precedence determine application. Inventory alone is insufficient.|Configured objects and resultant policy are different evidence.

lockout-window|E|E4|complexity|Why check the lockout observation/reset window as well as the threshold?|The counter's time behavior affects online guessing risk|The window changes the NT hash algorithm|The window assigns new SIDs to users|The threshold is unrelated to authentication attempts|Threshold, duration, reset behavior, and account exceptions influence test planning. Offline guessing has different mechanics.|A single threshold number is an incomplete lockout policy.

spray-v-brute|E|E4|authn|A tester tries one common password against many authorized accounts. What is this strategy called?|Password spraying|Per-account exhaustive brute force|A stored-hash birthday attack|A certificate-chain validation test|Spraying distributes attempts across accounts. It can still cause lockouts or alerts depending on policy and execution.|Distributing attempts does not remove operational risk.

lm-empty-half|E|E4|password|Why can an LM password with no second seven-byte half be easier to analyze?|One half has a known empty-input value|The NT hash reveals the password directly|The account's SID becomes the encryption key|The domain policy necessarily disables lockout|LM's independent halves and predictable empty component reduce work for some inputs. Actual password case needs separate evidence.|A structural weakness can narrow work without revealing every byte.

ntlm-relay-signing|E|E4|smb|How does requiring SMB signing help against certain SMB authentication relays?|It requires authenticated integrity for the session's messages|It changes every NT password hash into a salted hash|It makes every user a local administrator|It encrypts all traffic to every unrelated service|Signing binds message integrity to session key material. Relay exposure also depends on source/target protocol and policy.|An authentication protocol's safeguards depend on the destination service.

signing-encryption|E|E1|smb|What is the main distinction between SMB signing and SMB encryption?|Signing protects integrity; encryption adds confidentiality|Signing hides file content while encryption only lists shares|Both only conceal server names in DNS|Both replace all file permissions|These transport protections do not determine which files an account may access. Evaluate transport and authorization separately.|Integrity, confidentiality, and file access are separate properties.

share-ntfs|E|E1|smb|A share grants Full Control but NTFS grants the user read-only access. What is the usual combined result for that network access?|The more restrictive effective access applies|Share Full Control overrides all NTFS restrictions|NTFS checks are bypassed over SMB|The user receives SYSTEM automatically|Share and filesystem permissions constrain different layers of access. Group/deny entries and effective-access details still matter.|One permissive layer does not erase another restrictive layer.

admin-share|E|E1|smb|Why does discovering ADMIN$ not prove anonymous administrative access?|Share existence does not establish the caller's permission|Every share ending $ has no authentication|ADMIN$ always publishes every user's plaintext password|The dollar sign encrypts each directory listing|Administrative shares are conventional features. Authenticate and evaluate actual accessible operations and rights.|Hidden or administrative share names are not findings by themselves.

token-whoami|E|E5|netcmd|Why use whoami /all after obtaining command execution?|Inspect the actual identity, groups, and privileges|Change the domain's schema automatically|Dump the full ntds.dit file without rights|Prove every vulnerability on the host|Token inspection describes current authority. Privilege names and enabled states need interpretation, not just counting.|A shell prompt is not a privilege level.

service-path-quotes|E|E5|crest|Why is an unquoted service path insufficient alone to prove escalation?|Writable candidate paths and privileged execution must also exist|Every space in a path grants root access|Only the service's display name matters|The path becomes a DNS record automatically|Path parsing can create an opportunity, but permissions and lifecycle determine whether an attacker can use it.|A suspicious configuration needs an executable impact path.

service-config-write|E|E5|crest|A user can change a SYSTEM service's binary path and start it. What is the relevant risk?|Privileged execution of a user-selected binary|Only exposure of the service's friendly name|Automatic compromise of every trusted domain|Only a cosmetic desktop change|Service configuration authority can cross a privilege boundary when an attacker-controlled program is run. Confirm the actual rights and resulting identity.|Configuration writes can be code-execution authority.

scheduled-task|E|E5|crest|A high-privilege scheduled task executes a script writable by ordinary users. Which evidence is decisive?|Write access plus the task's execution identity and trigger|Only the task's descriptive name|Only the script's filename extension|Only the user's browser settings|The writable script can influence later privileged execution. Scheduling and execution restrictions affect practicality.|Connect control of bytes to a privileged consumer.

lsa-protection|E|E5|ad|Why can credential-dumping behavior vary across Windows hosts with the same account privilege?|OS protections, credential presence, and process policy differ|Administrator membership guarantees plaintext secrets on every host|All hosts necessarily cache the same users|LSASS is a browser cookie store|Protected processes and authentication configuration affect available material and permitted access. Observe the actual artifact rather than assuming a standard dump.|Privilege does not guarantee a particular credential representation exists.

offline-registry|E|E4|ad|Why might analysis of protected registry hive copies require more than the SAM hive alone?|Credential protection can depend on companion system data|The SAM is a plain CSV of all passwords|Every hive contains a complete independent plaintext copy|DNS records are the only decryption input|Credential storage includes protection and context across files/keys. Treat recovered material according to its actual format.|A file name is not a complete credential-recovery recipe.

wsus-inventory|E|E6|ad|A WSUS dashboard reports a host compliant. What should a tester still establish?|What products and updates that compliance view covers|That every third-party application is patched|That all exploitable paths are absent|That every device outside the domain is included|Patch compliance has an inventory and policy scope. Correlate missing components and other update mechanisms.|A dashboard is a view of defined criteria.

kb-applicability|E|E6|crest|An exploit targets a Windows build before a vendor fix. What is a sound next applicability check?|Compare current build/component and relevant fix state|Match only the computer's NetBIOS name|Match only the user-interface language|Treat any Windows installation as vulnerable|Version families, installed components, and cumulative fixes affect applicability. Public exploit existence is not confirmation.|A platform label is broader than an affected configuration.

rollback|E|E5|crest|Why record temporary account or configuration changes during authorized post-exploitation?|Enable verified cleanup and accurate residual-state reporting|Guarantee every action leaves no forensic trace|Replace the need for a findings report|Make the next test's scope automatically larger|Cleanup needs an inventory of what changed, its ownership, and the intended prior state. Never infer reversion solely from an absent error.|A successful command is not a cleanup receipt.

kiosk-file-dialog|E|E7|crest|A kiosk permits file-dialog navigation into sensitive local paths but blocks a desktop shortcut. What should testing evaluate?|The allowed application's alternate access and launch paths|Only the absence of the blocked shortcut|Only the wallpaper's configured filename|Only the kiosk's public web domain|Lockdown must constrain actual actions, not just menu presentation. File dialogs can expose other code or data paths.|A hidden interface is not comprehensive confinement.

citrix-session|E|E7|crest|Why does a shell launched inside a Citrix session not automatically equal host administrator access?|The process retains its actual session identity and token|Citrix always runs every command as SYSTEM|A remote display changes every file ACL|The shell's screen resolution determines its privilege|An interface escape may expand actions while remaining under the same user rights. Establish each privilege boundary separately.|Breaking out of UI restrictions is not necessarily privilege escalation.

exchange-auth-surface|E|E8|exchange|Exchange exposes a public login page. What should an authentication review cover beyond TLS?|Enumeration, throttling, MFA, and supported authentication paths|Only the certificate's visual padlock icon|Only the page's color scheme|Only whether the domain has an MX record|Transport protection does not validate the account workflows. Alternative endpoints may use different authentication behavior.|A protected channel can still carry a weak login process.

exchange-protocols|E|E8|exchange|Why inventory enabled Exchange client-access protocols?|Different endpoints can expose different authentication paths|All clients necessarily use one web form|Every enabled protocol has identical authorization logic|Protocols are chosen only by the DNS MX preference|Client and administrative surfaces can have different protection and exposure. Review those actually enabled and reachable.|One tested login route does not cover every route.

exchange-patch-chain|E|E8|exchange|A published Exchange exploit chain starts with a version-specific server flaw. What evidence is needed before claiming the chain applies?|Affected component/build and required preconditions|Only the presence of an Exchange banner|Only the existence of a mailbox|Only successful delivery of one email|A chain can depend on several versions, paths, identities, and configuration choices. Validate prerequisites rather than reusing a product-level label.|A named exploit chain is a hypothesis until its conditions match.

exchange-admin|E|E8|exchange|Why separate mailbox-user authorization from Exchange administration rights?|They grant different operations and resource scopes|Every mailbox owner is an Exchange administrator|Every administrator has every user's plaintext password|A mailbox's email address determines all server permissions|Administrative and end-user surfaces have different authorities. Review delegated rights and actual operations.|Access to one mailbox does not imply server-wide administration.

exchange-relay|E|E8|smtp|Why is receiving external mail not itself proof of an open relay?|Relay concerns forwarding between unauthorized third-party domains|Every receiving server must relay for any sender|An MX record grants everyone delivery administration|SMTP AUTH encrypts every message automatically|A server can accept mail for its hosted domains while refusing unrelated onward relay. Test the relevant sender/recipient case.|Inbound delivery and third-party relaying are different behavior.

common-app-exploit|E|E9|crest|A client application has public exploit code. What matters before choosing it for a controlled test?|Affected version, prerequisites, reliability, and allowed impact|Only the exploit's download count|Only its filename containing the product name|Only the victim's desktop theme|Review applicability and operational consequences. A public PoC can be incomplete, destructive, or target a different build.|Availability of code is not validation of the technique.

document-client-context|E|E9|crest|A malicious document would execute code as a user's application. What separates this from server-side compromise?|The execution entry point and user process context|The file's use of a TCP port number|The document's paper size|The server's MX priority|Client exploitation, host privilege escalation, and lateral access are distinct steps. Scope and test evidence must identify the actual context.|Distinguish where execution begins from where it might eventually lead.
